name: Võru / Werro-Estonian dialect
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

catalog_quote: § 11. Der Accent ist, wie im Ehstnischen überhaupt so auch hier, ein trochäischer, d.h. er trifft die erste, dritte und fünfte Sylbe, am stärksten die erste, schwächer die dritte, noch schwächer die fünfte, und ist an den beiden letzten wohl überhaupt kaum hörbar, wenn nicht noch eine unbetonte (vierte und sechste) darauf folgt, gleichsam als Folie, von welcher sich die vorhergehende betonte erst recht deutlich für das Ohr abhebt. So hört man z. B. inemine (Mensch) deutlich als Ditrochäus [...] aber in hobene hört man mehr einen Dactylus [...] als einen Amphimacer [...]; kodanikidele klingt wie [...] aber kodanikide nur wie [...] Diese Ordnung von betonten und unbetonten Sylben kann aber mancherlei Störungen erleiden, theils dadurch, dass durch Syncope zwei betonte Sylben an einander gerückt werden, theils dadurch, dass gewisse Flexions- und Ableitungssylben immer den Ton haben, ohne Rücksicht auf die Anzahl der vorhergehenden Sylben. So klingt katuse wie [...] rikkuze aber (statt rikkauze) wie [...] uskliku, söämeliku wie [...] weil die Ableitungssylbe lik (wie mik, tik, dik, rik und die erste Sylbe in kene, mane, mäne, lane, läne, line, mine) immer den Ton hat. Die Stelle des Nebentones ist auch in der Formenlehre von grosser Wichtigkeit
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: § 11. Der Accent ist, wie im Ehstnischen überhaupt so auch hier, ein trochäischer, d.h. er trifft die erste, dritte und fünfte Sylbe, am stärksten die erste, schwächer die dritte, noch schwächer die fünfte, und ist an den beiden letzten wohl überhaupt kaum hörbar, wenn nicht noch eine unbetonte (vierte und sechste) darauf folgt [...] Diese Ordnung von betonten und unbetonten Sylben kann aber mancherlei Störungen erleiden, theils dadurch, dass durch Syncope zwei betonte Sylben an einander gerückt werden, theils dadurch, dass gewisse Flexions- und Ableitungssylben immer den Ton haben, ohne Rücksicht auf die Anzahl der vorhergehenden Sylben.
new_statements.translation: § 11. The accent is, as in Estonian generally, so also here [in Võru Estonian], a trochaic one, i.e. it falls on the first, third and fifth syllable, most strongly on the first, weaker on the third, still weaker on the fifth, and on the latter two is hardly audible at all unless a further unstressed syllable (fourth and sixth) follows [...] This ordering of stressed and unstressed syllables can however suffer various disturbances, partly because syncope brings two stressed syllables next to each other, partly because certain inflectional and derivational syllables always carry the stress regardless of the number of preceding syllables.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the word-initial syllable; rhythmic (trochaic) secondary stresses on the 3rd and 5th syllables. Confirmed by the modern primary description Pajusalu 2000 (Võru vokaalid I, p. 77, Vastseliina Võru and Karksi Mulgi): 'Pearõhuline silp on reeglina sõna esisilp' = 'the primary-stressed syllable is as a rule the first syllable of the word', and by Iva 2007: 239 (even loanwords normally take main stress on the first syllable).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Wiedemann §11: secondary stresses on odd-numbered syllables (3rd, 5th), progressively weaker; certain derivational suffixes (-lik, -mik, -tik, -dik, -rik, and the first syllable of -kene, -mane, -mäne, -reader, -läne, -line, -mine) always bear the (secondary) stress irrespective of syllable count, e.g. uskliku, söämeliku; Iva 2005: 130 likewise counts feet 'from the secondary stress' in tetrasyllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Wiedemann: syncope can juxtapose two stressed syllables; fixed-stress suffixes shift the secondary-stress rhythm; stronger accent ('schwerer Accent') used to distinguish partitive/illative from genitive (a quantity/Q3 phenomenon, not a change of stress position). Iva 2007: 239 'tavaliselt' (usually) for loanwords implies some recent loans may keep non-initial stress. Pajusalu & Teras 2003 intro table notes main stress can fall on a clitic ('Kliitikul pearõhk') in Võru/Setu.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in simple (non-compound) words; Wiedemann describes citation/word forms of the 'Werro-Ehstnisch' (Võru) dialect; Pajusalu 2000 statement is for spontaneous dialect speech of Vastseliina (East Võru) and Karksi (Mulgi).
new_statements.identity_note: Wiedemann 1864 describes the 'werroehstnische Dialekt' = Võru (Võro) South Estonian as spoken in the 19th c. (Võru county parishes), i.e. the core of sout2679. Pajusalu 2000's corroborating sentence covers Vastseliina (East Võru, sout2679) together with Karksi (Mulgi dialect, which Glottolog files under a separate South Estonian sub-branch: mulg1234?—treat the Karksi half as a different variety). Seto (also commonly subsumed under vro/sout2679) is not separately covered by the quoted statement.

tone_statements.citation: Norvik, Miina, Uldis Balodis, Valts Ernštreits, Gunta Kļava, Helle Metslang, Karl Pajusalu & Eva Saar. 2021. The South Estonian language islands in the context of the Central Baltic area. Eesti ja soome-ugri keeleteaduse ajakiri / Journal of Estonian and Finno-Ugric Linguistics 12(2): 33–72. doi:10.12697/jeful.2021.12.2.02
tone_statements.quote: Tonal variation is not typical of the Finno-Ugric languages. Broken tone or stød is characteristic, however, of Latvian and Latgalian, and is also found in Livonian (e.g., lē’ḑ [leːˀdʲ] ‘leaf; page’). In addition to Livonian, broken tone is also found in Leivu and Lutsi, e.g., Leivu vähämb [ˈvæ.hæmb] > vä’ämb [væːˀmb] ‘less’ … Lutsi hi’ir [hiːˀr] ‘mouse’ (in which broken tone is connected with the third quantity degree), rehe [ˈre.he] > re’e [reːˀ] ‘threshing barn’ (see Balodis et al. 2016), but it has not been observed in other South Estonian dialects or in Kraasna.
tone_statements.locator: p. 60, §4 Phonological features (paragraph after Table 7; discussion continues to p. 61)
tone_statements.summary: Broken tone (stød) occurs only sporadically in the Leivu and Lutsi language islands, partly tied to h-loss and the third quantity degree; absent in Võro, Seto and Kraasna; no tone inventory stated.

tone_statements.citation: Teras, Pire & Tuuli Tuisk. 2021. Broken tone in Livonian and Leivu. In Proceedings of the 1st International Conference on Tone and Intonation (TAI 2021), Sønderborg, 26–30. ISCA. doi:10.21437/TAI.2021-6
tone_statements.quote: It appears that such a loss can result in minimal pairs, e.g., maa [mɑːː] (plain tone, Q31) ‘land’ vs. maha > ma’a [mɑːːˀ]2 (broken tone, Q3) ‘land, sg.ill; down’. … The process and materials of the current study show that it is somewhat difficult to provide any definite conclusions on the phonological status of the broken tone in Leivu. The lack of sufficient amount of test words makes it impossible to claim that broken tone has the same role in Leivu as in Livonian.
tone_statements.locator: p. 27, section 1 Introduction (first part) and p. 29, end of section 3.3 Intensity and laryngealisation (part after the ellipsis)
tone_statements.summary: Leivu words that lost /h/ carry a stød-like broken tone opposed to plain tone (maa vs ma’a), cued by an early F0 peak in the stressed syllable; few words; authors leave its phonological status open.

tone_statements.citation: Teras, Pire. 2021. Broken tone in Leivu CV’V-words. Eesti ja soome-ugri keeleteaduse ajakiri / Journal of Estonian and Finno-Ugric Linguistics 12(2): 169–190. Tartu: University of Tartu Press.
tone_statements.quote: Broken tone or stød is one of the innovations that the South Estonian Leivu dialect shares with another Finnic language – Livonian (Viitso 2009). [...] Broken tone found in Latvian – as well as in Livonian, Lithuanian, and Danish – was also developing in Leivu South Estonian. [...] In some cases, the final part of the syllable nucleus is laryngealised in CV’V words. Fundamental frequency in accented CV’V-words is almost always falling (an early F0 TP occurring at 23% of the total duration of the syllable rhyme).
tone_statements.summary: Leivu South Estonian was developing a restricted broken-tone (stød) contrast on long stressed syllables that lost intervocalic /h/ (CV’V vs plain Q3 CVV): falling F0 with early peak, intensity dip, sometimes laryngealisation; a marginal contact-induced tonal feature, not a general lexical tone system.

tone_statements.citation: Balodis, Uldis, Karl Pajusalu & Pire Teras. 2016. Broken tone in South Estonian dialects in Latvia. Linguistica Lettica 24: 98–114. Rīga: Latvian Language Institute, University of Latvia.
tone_statements.quote: If an intervocalic h is lost, these words are pronounced with broken tone, which is characterised by falling F0, an abrupt dip in intensity or an irregular intensity movement during the vowel, and secondarily by a laryngealization period during or at the end of the vowel. In Leivu and Lutsi stød appears usually as a sporadic manner of pronunciation which does not have a phonological status but instead suggests a language change in progress.
tone_statements.summary: Broken tone (stød) occurs sporadically in Leivu and Lutsi on long stressed-syllable vowels where intervocalic h (Lutsi also j) was lost: falling F0, intensity dip, creak; no phonological status.

tone_statements.citation: Viitso, Tiit-Rein. 2009. Livonian and Leivu: shared innovations and problems. Linguistica Uralica 45(4): 269–282. doi:10.3176/lu.2009.4.03
tone_statements.quote: … a drop (or even a break) of pitch and intensity. The latter property has induced the term BROKEN TONE. … In Leivu, *h is substituted with stød mostly in illative forms of monosyllabic vocalic stems and in stems where *h occurred between identical vowels, e.g. n∑a •a¿ ’skins’, pä•ä ’head (IllSg)’, r∑a •ad ’money (PSg)’ … In Leivu, stød was considered a tonal feature (an intonation) by Eberhard Winkler (1999 : 202) … Yet he is right, as also in Leivu the word r∑a •a ’money’ takes the partitive singular ending -d that occurs only with monosyllabic stems ending in a long monophthong, cf. r∑a •ad
tone_statements.summary: Leivu South Estonian has a broken tone (stød), a drop or break of pitch, in a few forms where intervocalic *h was lost (e.g. 'money', 'head' IllSg); argued tonal, not a segment. No inventory stated.

tone_statements.citation: Viitso, Tiit-Rein. 1990. Stress and quantity in North Setu (South Estonian). Linguistica Uralica 26(2): 81–88. Tallinn: Estonian Academy Publishers.
tone_statements.quote: the syllables of Q 1 have a rising pitch and those of Q 2 a rising-falling pitch, while syllables of Q 3 have a falling pitch that can be preceded by a short rise. [...] [the three distinctive quantities Q1, Q2, and Q3] in North Setu can be described by means of two pairs of features, viz. (a) a short vs. a long syllable and (b) a syllable marked with the light vs. the heavy syllabic accent [...] Stress is [a] component of accent, except in the negative aspect forms that have the primary stress on the final syllable
tone_statements.locator: p. 82 (sect. 2 Quantity) and p. 87 (sect. 4 Conclusions); stress rule p. 81 (sect. 1 Stress)
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone proper: the Q2/Q3 quantity contrast of stressed syllables is analysed as a light vs heavy syllabic accent with characteristic pitch contours (Q1 rising, Q2 rising-falling, Q3 falling), i.e. an accentual (quantity-cum-pitch) opposition confined to stressed syllables; primary stress normally word-initial.

sources.quote: XIII. Alle Woerter, sie moegen noch so vielsylbig seyn, haben den Ton auf der ersten Sylbe, die daher allezeit lang ausgesprochen wird. [Anm.] 1. In zusammengesetzten Woertern bleibt der Ton auf der ersten Sylbe eines jeden Worts, als jummala-kartmatta: wenn das letzte Wort einsylbig ist, so liegt der Ton zuweilen allein auf der ersten Sylbe des ersten Worts, wie in heina-koers. ... 5. Ausser den zusammengesetzten Woertern giebt es noch andre, welche die obige allgemeine Ton-Regel scheinbar oder wirklich einschraenken. ... 2) Etliche andre die auf der letzten Sylbe wegen des darin befindlichen doppelten Selbstlauters den Ton haben ... pallapool ... wikkerkaar ... 3) Etliche aus andern Sprachen entlehnte, z. B. sele ... wariseer (dreysylbig) ... wilistid die Philister, wo der Ton auf der mittelsten Sylbe ruht, obgleich der Ehste ihn auch hier gern auf die erste legt. ... Indessen legt der Ehste nicht auf alle fremde Woerter den Ton so wie sie ihn urspruenglich haben, sondern gern auf die erste Sylbe, welches er auch bey dem Namen Pilatus thut.

sources.note: Primary stress fixed on the first syllable of every word regardless of length; the stressed first syllable is 'allezeit lang ausgesprochen' (stress-length link). Compounds keep stress on the first syllable of each member (jummala-kartmatta); with a monosyllabic second member stress can fall only on the first member (heina-koers). tone.quote: Tonal variation is not typical of the Finno-Ugric languages. Broken tone or stød is characteristic, however, of Latvian and Latgalian, and is also found in Livonian (e.g., lē’ḑ [leːˀdʲ] ‘leaf; page’). In addition to Livonian, broken tone is also found in Leivu and Lutsi, e.g., Leivu vähämb [ˈvæ.hæmb] > vä’ämb [væːˀmb] ‘less’ … Lutsi hi’ir [hiːˀr] ‘mouse’ (in which broken tone is connected with the third quantity degree), rehe [ˈre.he] > re’e [reːˀ] ‘threshing barn’ (see Balodis et al. 2016), but it has not been observed in other South Estonian dialects or in Kraasna.

sources.quote: Broken tone or stød is one of the innovations that the South Estonian Leivu dialect shares with another Finnic language – Livonian (Viitso 2009). [...] Broken tone found in Latvian – as well as in Livonian, Lithuanian, and Danish – was also developing in Leivu South Estonian. [...] In some cases, the final part of the syllable nucleus is laryngealised in CV’V words. Fundamental frequency in accented CV’V-words is almost always falling (an early F0 TP occurring at 23% of the total duration of the syllable rhyme).
sources.note: Acoustic study (durations, F0, intensity) of Leivu words that lost intervocalic /h/ (CV’V) vs Q3 CVV monosyllables: an incipient broken tone (stød), a Latvian-type contact feature, restricted to long stressed syllables; realised as falling F0 with an early turning point, an intensity dip between the vowel portions and occasional laryngealisation. Reviews earlier claims (Niilus 1936, Kettunen 1938, Viitso 2009, Balodis, Pajusalu & Teras 2016) that Leivu and Lutsi South Estonian have broken tone.

tone.quote: Broken tone or stød is one of the innovations that the South Estonian Leivu dialect shares with another Finnic language – Livonian (Viitso 2009). [...] Broken tone found in Latvian – as well as in Livonian, Lithuanian, and Danish – was also developing in Leivu South Estonian. [...] In some cases, the final part of the syllable nucleus is laryngealised in CV’V words. Fundamental frequency in accented CV’V-words is almost always falling (an early F0 TP occurring at 23% of the total duration of the syllable rhyme).
tone.summary: Leivu South Estonian was developing a restricted broken-tone (stød) contrast on long stressed syllables that lost intervocalic /h/ (CV’V vs plain Q3 CVV): falling F0 with early peak, intensity dip, sometimes laryngealisation; a marginal contact-induced tonal feature, not a general lexical tone system.
tone.says: Acoustic study (durations, F0, intensity) of Leivu words that lost intervocalic /h/ (CV’V) vs Q3 CVV monosyllables: an incipient broken tone (stød), a Latvian-type contact feature, restricted to long stressed syllables; realised as falling F0 with an early turning point, an intensity dip between the vowel portions and occasional laryngealisation. Reviews earlier claims (Niilus 1936, Kettunen 1938, Viitso 2009, Balodis, Pajusalu & Teras 2016) that Leivu and Lutsi South Estonian have broken tone.

sources.citation: Balodis, Uldis, Karl Pajusalu & Pire Teras. 2016. Broken tone in South Estonian dialects in Latvia. Linguistica Lettica 24: 98–114. Rīga: Latvian Language Institute, University of Latvia.
sources.quote: If an intervocalic h is lost, these words are pronounced with broken tone, which is characterised by falling F0, an abrupt dip in intensity or an irregular intensity movement during the vowel, and secondarily by a laryngealization period during or at the end of the vowel. In Leivu and Lutsi stød appears usually as a sporadic manner of pronunciation which does not have a phonological status but instead suggests a language change in progress.
sources.note: Broken tone (stød) occurs sporadically in Leivu and Lutsi on long stressed-syllable vowels where intervocalic h (Lutsi also j) was lost: falling F0, intensity dip, creak; no phonological status.

sources.quote: … a drop (or even a break) of pitch and intensity. The latter property has induced the term BROKEN TONE. … In Leivu, *h is substituted with stød mostly in illative forms of monosyllabic vocalic stems and in stems where *h occurred between identical vowels, e.g. n∑a •a¿ ’skins’, pä•ä ’head (IllSg)’, r∑a •ad ’money (PSg)’ … In Leivu, stød was considered a tonal feature (an intonation) by Eberhard Winkler (1999 : 202) … Yet he is right, as also in Leivu the word r∑a •a ’money’ takes the partitive singular ending -d that occurs only with monosyllabic stems ending in a long monophthong, cf. r∑a •ad
sources.note: Leivu South Estonian has a broken tone (stød), a drop or break of pitch, in a few forms where intervocalic *h was lost (e.g. 'money', 'head' IllSg); argued tonal, not a segment. No inventory stated.

sources.citation: Viitso, Tiit-Rein. 1990. Stress and quantity in North Setu (South Estonian). Linguistica Uralica 26(2): 81–88. Tallinn: Estonian Academy Publishers.
sources.quote: the syllables of Q 1 have a rising pitch and those of Q 2 a rising-falling pitch, while syllables of Q 3 have a falling pitch that can be preceded by a short rise. [...] [the three distinctive quantities Q1, Q2, and Q3] in North Setu can be described by means of two pairs of features, viz. (a) a short vs. a long syllable and (b) a syllable marked with the light vs. the heavy syllabic accent [...] Stress is [a] component of accent, except in the negative aspect forms that have the primary stress on the final syllable
sources.locator: p. 82 (sect. 2 Quantity) and p. 87 (sect. 4 Conclusions); stress rule p. 81 (sect. 1 Stress)
sources.note: Phonological analysis of stress and the three quantities in North Setu: quantities occur only in stressed syllables; Q1/Q2/Q3 stressed syllables carry rising / rising-falling / falling pitch; Q2 vs Q3 analysed as a light vs heavy syllabic 'accent' (following Tauli 1973), with stress a component of accent; North Setu uniquely has Q2 monosyllables and negative verb forms with primary stress on the final syllable (marked with an additional specific stress).

sources.note: Acoustic study of Leivu quantity: F0 peak is late in Q1/Q2 and early in Q3 words, and a few words show stød (early F0 peak plus laryngealization); no tone system or tone inventory is stated.

tone.quote: The fundamental frequency analysis showed that Q1 and Q2 words were characterized by a late F0 peak in the first syllable and Q3 words by an early F0 peak. Even if the duration ratios in Q2 and Q3 words overlapped, the two quantities were differentiated by the location of F0 peak. There were only some words where stød was expected. These words were characterized by an early F0 turning point and almost always by a laryngealization period.

tone.quote: In most examples, the loss of short h has caused stød at the syllable boundary, e.g. r∑a’à ~ râ ’money’, v∑ä’^ämb ’less’ … This can be compared to stød in Latvian and Livonian. … The fundamental frequency analysis showed that Q1 and Q2 words were characterised by a late F0 peak in the first syllable and Q3 words by an early F0 peak. Even if the duration ratios in Q2 and Q3 words overlapped, the two quantities were differentiated by the location of F0 peak. Only one word pronounced with laryngealization was found in the present data.
